Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP National disability insurance scheme Pocock and crossbenchers call Labor’s NDIS overhaul ‘too far, too fast’ in scathing Senate inquiry report Greens say Labor’s reform set to ‘rip life-changing supports away from disabled people instead of raising additional revenue through taxing gas exports’ Sarah Basford Canales and Krishani Dhanji Fri 14 Aug 2026 04.04 EDT Last modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 04.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Cross-benchers have slammed the Albanese government’s proposed overhaul of the NDIS as going “too far, too fast” as the changes to curb the growth of the $52bn program appear set to pass the parliament as early as next week. The Greens and independent ACT senator, David Pocock , delivered scathing assessments of the bill they warn will enable blunt and indiscriminate cuts to individual budgets supporting more than 770,000 Australians with disabilities in a final Senate inquiry report released on Friday afternoon. The NDIS has given Joe vital social skills. Funding cuts leave his mother fearing how he will ‘do life’ Read more While the Labor-chaired committee recommended the bill pass, Greens senator Jordon Steele-John said the proposals would be “devastating to the lives of disabled people and their families”. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The bill forms part of the government’s plan to get the NDIS “back on track” and save $37.8bn over four years by tightening the eligibility criteria and subjecting all participants to independent functional assessments from 2028. It will also give the NDIS minister, Mark Butler, the power to reduce funding categories for individuals by up to 99%. The government has already said it will apply a 50% reduction in individual participant budgets for social, civic and community participation. Without the interventions, the government estimates the $52bn-a-year scheme will more than double in cost to $117bn a year in a decade’s time. The Greens have acknowledged some changes should be made to make the NDIS work better for participants but suggested the scheme could be funded by a gas export tax. “The choice that this Labor government is making is to rip life-changing supports away from disabled people instead of raising additional revenue through taxing gas exports shows their priorities clearly,” Steele-John wrote. “This government is choosing the profits of large corporations over the lives of disabled people.” Guardian Australia has previously reported that 241,000 NDIS participants will be shifted off the scheme by June 2031 after the introduction of the functional capacity test, to keep the number of participants at about 600,000. During that period, an additional 105,000 will be stopped from entering the scheme. Those shifted from the scheme are expected to be supported by programs run by states and territories with joint funding from the Commonwealth. Pocock said no participant should be removed from the NDIS until those new programs are “funded, operating and accessible”, vowing to continue scrutiny of the changes. “The true measure of these changes will be found in the experiences of people with disability. They must remain at the centre of what comes next,” Pocock said. Coalition senators provided additional comments raising concerns that fraud and integrity within the NDIS had not been sufficiently addressed. The government is expected to land a deal with the opposition early next week in order to pass the bill in the Senate. Disability advocacy groups have been extremely critical of the government’s amendments to the NDIS, and have warned caring responsibilities will be shifted from the scheme to families, affecting women disproportionately. Women With Disabilities Australia’s chief executive, Sophie Cusworth, said the government should deliver a comprehensive gender impact assessment of the bill. “You cannot say you are working for women while looking to pass legislation that puts women’s safety, care, health and economic security at risk,” she said on Friday. “That is not gender equality. https://www.dw.com/en/in-saxony-anhalt-e.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JIs8 Saxony-Anhalt is governed from the state parliament in Magdeburg Image: ArTo/Zoonar/IMAGO Advertisement It's rare that a state parliament election in Germany attracts as much media interest as this one in Saxony-Anhalt . On Sunday, the 1.7 million eligible voters in the eastern German state will decide whether the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party can form a state government for the first time. There hasn't been a head of government who belonged to a proven far-right party in post- World War II Germany — at neither federal nor state level. That would change if AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund were to be elected to this position, since the Office for the Protection of the Constitution in Saxony-Anhalt already classified the AfD as such in 2023. Siegmund's chances of a historical triumph are high: For months, the AfD has been comfortably leading the polls with well over 40% of the vote. AfD, CDU and Left Party will get into parliament Aside from the AfD, there are only two other parties that can count on being included in the next state parliament: The conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of current State Premier Sven Schulze and the socialist Left Party , which is traditionally strong in eastern Germany, the former socialist GDR . All other parties have cause for concern: they could fail to reach the 5% threshold of votes necessary for entry into parliaments in Germany. This even applies to the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), who currently form part of the federal government coalition with the CDU and its Bavarian counterpart, the Christian Social Union (CSU). SPD, Greens, FDP, BSW might not make the 5% mark The SPD is losing popularity nationwide . In Saxony-Anhalt, they are polling below the 8% they won five years ago. The third party in Saxony-Anhalt's current governing coalition, formed in 2021, has even fewer hopes: The neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP) are polling only about 3%. Following the FDP's failure in the Bundestag general election of 2025 and multiple defeats at the state level, supporters are bracing themselves for the next setback. The environmentalist Greens may also not return to the state parliament. The party, whose core voter base is in wealthy western German cities, is vehemently rejected by many voters in rural areas because of its climate policies and multicultural vision of society. Concern over Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance And then there is the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), founded in 2024 by its namesake, a former Left Party co-leader. The party is economically left-leaning, but socially right-wing conservative and populist. This is its first time participating in a state election in Saxony-Anhalt. After the BSW gained 6.2% of the vote in the European Parliament elections in 2024 and won results of between about 12% and 16% in the eastern German states of Brandenburg, Saxony and Thuringia during its first year, it failed by only a few thousand votes to reach the 5% hurdle to enter German parliament in the 2025 general election. The BSW never really recovered from this setback, and it went on to be defeated in three further state parliament elections. The party also has cause for concern in Saxony-Anhalt, where it has been polling under 5%. Should it win representation after all, Sahra Wagenknecht has already announced that her party's lawmakers would not vote an AfD premier into office, but abstain from the vote — paving the way for him to win a majority in parliament and take office. Considering the poor polling numbers for the BSW in Saxony-Anhalt, political scientist Oliver Lembcke speaks of an "endgame" for the party as a whole. What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Small parties could prevent absolute majority for AfD The fact is: The more parties fail to reach the threshold, the higher the likelihood that the Alternative for Germany will be able to govern alone. On the other hand, if aside from the AfD, the CDU, Left Party and SPD win representation in the next Saxony-Anhalt parliament, and those three parties together hold more seats than the AfD, the situation is complicated. In 2018, the CDU adopted a so-called " resolution of incompatibility ," which rejects cooperation with both the AfD and the Left Party. If the CDU sticks to this resolution, forming even a minority government would be very difficult, perhaps impossible. Could the CDU form a minority government? Political scientist Lembcke from Ruhr University Bochum argues that the CDU should have adapted its incompatibility resolution to the changed conditions of the party systems and political landscape. Because it has failed to do so, this issue could now escalate drastically in Saxony-Anhalt. The Left Party is prepared to support State Premier Sven Schulze of the CDU to secure a second term. "In recent years, we, the Left Party, have shown that we take responsibility for this country. Especially when it comes to inhibiting the AfD," Left Party co-leader Luigi Pantisano told television broadcaster ZDF. Pantisano pointed to the states of Thuringia and Saxony , where the CDU leads coalition governments without a parliamentary majority and depends on the support of the Left Party. Given the foreseeably complicated situation, one thing is clear ahead of the September 6 election: either Saxony-Anhalt faces an incredibly difficult coalition-building process, or the state will be governed by the AfD — if the party profits from the failure of many small parties and thereby receives an absolute majority in the state parliament. Photograph: Dado Ruvić/Reuters View image in fullscreen There have been calls to ban the use of Palantir’s software by the Australian government since May. Photograph: Dado Ruvić/Reuters National disability insurance scheme NDIS data may have ended up in Palantir’s analytics platform as part of efforts to curb fraud Exclusive: The Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission, which has access to NDIA data, used Palantir as part of a multi-agency fraud taskforce Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Josh Taylor Technology reporter Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.09 EDT Last modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.34 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Personal information of national disability insurance scheme participants may have ended up in controversial software company Palantir’s analytics platform as part of a massive multi-agency sharing program investigating fraud, Guardian Australia can reveal. There have been calls to ban the use of Palantir’s software by the Australian government since May , after it implied some cultures are inferior to others in a manifesto described by one UK MP as the “ramblings of a supervillain”. Last month, the National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) denied using Palantir’s software, following questions from Guardian Australia after a freedom of information request revealed the agency had met with representatives of the company co-founded by US Trump-aligned billionaire Peter Thiel in 2023. However, Guardian Australia can reveal data from the agency is being shared with the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission (ACIC), which has used Palantir as part of the Fraud Fusion Taskforce of 25 government agencies that is responsible for investigating fraud. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The taskforce – established in 2022 – is led by the NDIA and Services Australia, while the ACIC is responsible for the Fraud Fusion Centre, which brings in “large volumes of information, data and intelligence” held by agencies that could be relevant to the taskforce’s work, according to documents released under freedom of information. Calls grow to ban Palantir in Australia after manifesto described by UK MP as ‘ramblings of a supervillain’ Read more The ACIC last year said the agency was using “a range of specialist tools … to gather intelligence, advanced data analysis” to “identify behavioural patterns and financial activity, and access to extensive intelligence databases that provide deep insights into serious and organised crime networks”. ACIC has paid millions in contracts to Palantir in the past few years for its software to map connections between people, and the FoI docs suggest ACIC’s capabilities include bulk data analytics and data-matching across participating agencies’ databases. Gabrielle Josling, a data scientist and researcher, who filed a number of the freedom of information requests to participating agencies in the taskforce, attempted to obtain from the ACIC records of data from the fraud taskforce or centre being fed into Palantir’s software. In correspondence from late August, an FoI officer revealed reluctance to process the request given “the process for ingesting one FFC dataset into Palantir generates an amount of documents that … would likely not be manageable”. A spokesperson for the NDIA confirmed it was sharing participant information with the taskforce. “NDIS participant information is only shared with Fraud Fusion Taskforce partners on a restricted basis where potential criminal conduct is suspected to protect participants from fraud,” a spokesperson said. A spokesperson for the ACIC said it used “a suite of analytical tools and capabilities” and taskforce-related data collected and stored by the ACIC is consistent with the restrictions agreed with the provisioning agency. “The contributing agency is responsible for articulating any use, handling, and disclosure restrictions to the ACIC.” Tom Sulston, the head of policy at Digital Rights Watch, said it was “very concerning” if Palantir was being used in the assessment of potential fraud in the NDIS and similar programs. “People using NDIS deserve the dignity of not being treated like criminals simply for accessing the services that they need to live a full life,” he said. “The creation of such enormous aggregated datasets is a fundamentally de-humanising application of surveillance technology. That’s particularly awful when targeted at people living with disabilities, who are already regularly subjected to regular dehumanisation and indignities.” The Greens senator and digital rights and AI spokesperson, David Shoebridge, said the FoI response revealed that “having Palantir inside any one government agency sees millions of data points ingested by this global surveillance vampire”. “NDIS participants give their data to the agency believing it will be protected and only used to assist in their claims, having it funnelled into Palantir under the guise of fraud prevention is a deep betrayal.” A spokesperson for Palantir said the company “builds software that helps organisations use their data to make better decisions and solve their most complex problems”. “We are committed to supporting Australian government agencies in tackling complex challenges, including serious financial crime and fraud.” The supermarket giant Coles announced last week it would not extend its contract with Palantir beyond 2027. Coles had used Palantir software in rostering, store operations and supply chain planning. https://vietnamnews.vn/life-style/179893.text: Film project explores overseas Vietnamese's journey to roots PRAGUE — Beyond the Broken Bridge, an international film project exploring the identity, family, and journey of Vietnamese people living abroad to reconnect with their roots, was introduced by Cinexia Productions at the Vietnam–Europe Film Gala in Prague, Czech Republic, on September 3. According to directors Alex Werner, Kristina Schippling and Zhong To, the Sapa shopping centre was chosen as one of the film’s first shooting locations because it is home to a large Vietnamese community in Prague, where Vietnamese culture and community life are strongly visible in the heart of Europe. Werner said he was impressed by the centre, which gives him the feeling of a “miniature Hà Nội” in Europe. Its people, daily life and business activities provide authentic material for the film. The crew has also been recruiting actors and Vietnamese shopkeepers, workers, young people and families for supporting roles and crowd scenes. Rather than simply telling a story about returning to Việt Nam, Beyond the Broken Bridge delves into questions of identity and where people truly belong to. Co-director Zhong To said many Vietnamese who grow up abroad have to harmonise family and community values passed down from previous generations and Western environments that place greater emphasis on individualism. The differences can create gaps between generations, he said, but also provide material for the film to explore Vietnamese identity in a multicultural society. Co-director Kristina Schippling, a Berlin-based writer and filmmaker, said the international perspective of the filmmaking team is expected to help bring the story of the overseas Vietnamese community to international audiences. After Prague, the crew plans to film in HCM City, Đà Nẵng, Múi Né and Hà Nội before returning to Prague next January for winter scenes. Zhong To said the film seeks to offer a deeper perspective on Vietnamese people beyond familiar images of food and culture, focusing instead on migrant family life, generational divides and the search for a place to belong to. Through Beyond the Broken Bridge, the team hopes to bring the stories of Vietnamese living abroad closer to international audiences while contributing to cinematic and cultural exchanges between Việt Nam and Europe. — VNA/VNS Life & Style Vietnam iContent2026 highlights positive digital contents, encourages healthy digital environment Life & Style Why Phú Quốc is winning over high end Russian travellers Life & Style A documentary about digital transformation in education won a short film contest Life & Style Hà Nội shares common points with jazz, both look to further development in the country Life & Style Localities work to expand Laos–Việt Nam–Thailand tourism links Life & Style Hội An lanterns bring Vietnamese colours to Hong Kong Mid-Autumn Festival Life & Style Vietnamese Silk Rhapsody - Symphony of Vietnamese Silk held in HCM City "Vietnamese Silk Rhapsody - Symphony of Vietnamese Silk" took centre stage last night in HCM City, presenting a special artistic show that seamlessly blended traditional Vietnamese music, the enchanting sound of the zither, the beauty of silk, the elegance of áo dài, high-end fashion, and captivating contemporary performances.
